answer.exemplar: A syllogism is an argument with exactly two terms and two premises, where the two premises together yield the conclusion. The major term is the term that appears as the predicate of the conclusion, the minor term is the term that appears as the subject of the conclusion, and the middle term is the one that appears in both premises but not in the conclusion. The middle term is what makes the reasoning a syllogism at all, since it is the only term that does duty in both premises, and dropping it leaves two statements that share no content and can be true or false independently. Recognising the two terms and the middle term is what makes a syllogism analysable, because once they are identified one can check whether the two premises really do force the conclusion or whether the argument only appears to do so.

answer.exemplar: An enthymeme is an argument with one of its premises left unstated, usually because the missing premise is regarded as obvious. Classical examples run: all Greeks are human, all humans are mortal, therefore all Greeks are mortal, with the second premise suppressed because no one doubts it. The danger is that the suppressed premise is doing real work and may not be shared, so the same skeleton can carry a valid inference for one audience and an invalid one for another. A speaker who uses an enthymeme without naming its missing premise is therefore committing an argument to the audience's unstated agreement, and a reader who reconstructs the enthymeme must supply that premise before deciding whether the conclusion follows. The form is worth recognising precisely because nothing on the page marks where the argument stops and inference begins.

questions.explanation: A model answer must name the suppressed premise and then say why its absence is a problem, which is that the inference is only valid given that premise. An answer that gives an example but never identifies the missing premise does not satisfy the item, and neither does one that claims the argument is invalid for that reason alone, since it may well be valid once the premise is supplied.

answer.exemplar: From a contradiction, once you have asserted a statement and its negation, any further statement follows, and this is the principle of explosion, sometimes called ex falso quodlibet. The reason is structural rather than magical. Any argument form that is valid already lets a false premise yield a false conclusion, and a contradiction supplies both a statement and its negation, so the premises of any form can be satisfied by choosing the right truth values; since the form is valid, the conclusion is then forced. In practice the inference is a warning that a system allowing contradictions has lost the ability to distinguish conclusions worth believing, which is why a consistent formal system is valued and why classical logic quietly assumes you have not asserted a contradiction. The principle matters in argument practice too, since an opponent who contradicts themselves has, in this sense, licensed every conclusion, though the useful response is to point out the contradiction rather than to exploit it.

questions.explanation: A model answer must give the reason, not just the claim, so the explanation has to say that validity alone forces the conclusion once the premises can be made true, and a contradiction does exactly that. Then it must say what is lost as a result, that the ability to distinguish conclusions worth believing, which is the point about inconsistency. An answer that merely reports the principle without the reason or the consequence does not satisfy the item.
questions.hint: Ask what validity alone forces when the premises can be made true by a contradiction.
